summary: Describes 6rd, which lets a service provider rapidly deploy IPv6 to IPv4 customer sites. It builds on 6to4 and uses stateless IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation to cross IPv4-only infrastructure. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: 6rd lets a service provider give its customers IPv6 addresses and carry the traffic across the provider's IPv4 network. It works by wrapping IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets and using the provider's own IPv6 prefix, so each provider handles only its own customers' traffic.

questions: how do isps deploy ipv6 over ipv4
can 6rd work with private ipv4 addresses
subtitle: Giving IPv6 customers native addresses over an IPv4 network, without new routing plans.

tldr.problem: Service providers that hand out routers to their customers can offer IPv6 quickly, but the 6to4 mechanism they would naturally reuse cannot guarantee that traffic from the native IPv6 Internet reaches those customers.
tldr.mechanism: 6rd keeps the stateless encapsulation of 6to4 but replaces the fixed 2002::/16 prefix with an IPv6 prefix the provider owns, so packets entering its gateways are only packets for its own customers.
tldr.outcome: The document reports one provider adding 6rd to its customer routers and offering IPv6 to more than 1,500,000 residential sites in five weeks, using no new number assignment.

today: RFC 5569 is an Informational Independent Submission published in January 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a mechanism rather than a standard, and the text reports how one provider used it to offer IPv6 to more than 1,500,000 residential customers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document starts with a deployment. A major French service provider in the Iliad group, called Free, took six steps between 7 November and 11 December 2007, five weeks in total: it obtained a /32 IPv6 prefix from its regional Internet registry, added 6rd support to the software of its Freebox home gateway by reusing available 6to4 code, provisioned a platform with a 6to4 gateway program and modified it for 6rd, tested IPv6 operation with several operating systems and applications, deployed the new downloadable software, and announced IPv6 connectivity at no extra charge to every customer who wanted to activate it.

More than 1,500,000 residential customers were then able to use IPv6, with native IPv6 addresses routed in IPv6. The only condition was that they activated IPv6 in their Freebox and on their own hosts. The point of the story is that a provider that supplies customer equipment with routing capability, and that has postponed IPv6, can stop waiting because 6rd cuts the investment and operating cost.

In December 2007 IPv6 availability was limited to one IPv6 link per customer site, with /64 site prefix assignments. A few months later, after the provider had reported the achievement and its plans to its registry and obtained a /26 prefix, up to 16 IPv6 links per customer became possible with /60 site prefix assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: The document opens with a report of one provider that added IPv6 to the routers it already supplies to homes, and reached more than 1.5 million customers in five weeks. The customers only had to switch IPv6 on.

sections.title: Problem Statement and Purpose of 6rd
sections.content:
Offering IPv6 alongside IPv4 at no extra charge breaks a deadlock that has delayed IPv6 deployment. Providers wait for customer demand, customers do not demand IPv6 while application vendors say their products work on the existing IPv4 infrastructure, and vendors keep investing in ways to work around address translation instead of in IPv6. Providers will not do this without very limited cost, and the providers best placed are those that supply routers to their customers: they can upgrade those routers and operate a gateway between their IPv4 infrastructure and the global IPv6 Internet, and they need no routing plans beyond the ones their IPv4 network already has.

Encapsulation as specified for 6to4 comes close to being sufficient. It is simple, supported on many platforms including personal computers, has portable open source code, and its stateless nature gives good scalability. One limitation of 6to4 stops a provider using it for full IPv6 unicast connectivity to its customers. A provider running 6to4 can guarantee that IPv6 packets leaving its customer sites reach the IPv6 Internet, and that packets from other 6to4 sites reach its customers, but it cannot guarantee that packets from native IPv6 sites reach them. A packet from a native IPv6 address must pass through a 6to4 relay router that does the encapsulation, and there is no guarantee that routes toward such a relay exist from everywhere, nor that all such relays forward toward the complete IPv4 Internet.

There is a second problem with running 6to4 relays. A provider that opens IPv6 routes toward its relays for the 6to4 prefix 2002::/16 may receive packets destined for an unknown number of other 6to4 providers. If it does not forward them, it creates a black hole in which packets are systematically lost. If it does forward them, it can no longer size its relays in proportion to the traffic of its own customers, and quality of service for those other providers is then hardly guaranteed.

6rd exists to remove this limitation. The purpose is that packets coming from the global Internet into the gateways of a provider are only packets destined for that provider's customer sites, and that all IPv6 packets destined for those customer sites, coming from anywhere on the IPv6 Internet, traverse a gateway of that provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The reason 6rd exists is a gap in 6to4. A 6to4 customer can reach the IPv6 Internet and can be reached from other 6to4 users, but not reliably from native IPv6 sites. A provider that also runs 6to4 relays has to carry other providers' traffic to keep the network consistent. 6rd narrows the job to the provider's own customers.

sections.title: Specification
sections.content:
6rd modifies 6to4 in three ways. First, the 6to4 functions are changed so that the fixed 6to4 prefix 2002::/16 is replaced by an IPv6 prefix from the provider's own address space, and the 6to4 anycast address is replaced by another anycast address chosen by the provider. Second, the provider operates one or more 6rd gateways, which are upgraded 6to4 routers, at the border between its IPv4 infrastructure and the IPv6 Internet. Third, the customer equipment supports IPv6 on the customer side of the link and 6rd, an upgraded 6to4 function, on the provider side.

The IPv6 prefix of a customer site is derived from the site's IPv4 address: the provider's 6rd relay IPv6 prefix, which is 32 bits or fewer, is followed by the 32-bit IPv4 address of the customer site, giving a site prefix of 64 bits or fewer. The chosen address format uses 32 bits of the IPv4 address in the IPv6 address, for simplicity and compatibility with the existing 6to4 code. Restricting the sites to one IPv6 subnet each was a consequence of the provider's initial /32 prefix; a provider with several registry-allocated IPv4 prefixes, as the one in the example had six with lengths from /10 to /16, could have implemented variable-length mapping tables, but that would have extended some of the IPv4 addressing entropy to the gateways and equipment and made the design significantly more complex, which would have defeated the goal of simplicity.

IPv6 traffic between two customer sites of the same provider crosses the provider's IPv4 infrastructure directly. When the equipment sees that the IPv6 destination of an outgoing packet starts with its own provider's 6rd relay prefix, it takes the 32 bits that follow that prefix as the IPv4 destination of the encapsulating packet, applying the sending and decapsulation rules of 6to4 with the 6rd prefix in place of the 6to4 prefix.

Each provider may choose its own IPv4 anycast address for its 6rd relays, with the single constraint that routes advertised toward the provider must not include that address. The provider in the example took 192.88.99.201, routed with the same /24 prefix as 6to4 but with 201 instead of 1, to avoid confusion with 192.88.99.1, the 6to4 anycast address.
sections.plainLanguage: 6rd takes a customer's IPv4 address and puts it after the provider's own IPv6 prefix, so each customer gets a real IPv6 address. Traffic is wrapped in IPv4, sent over the provider's existing network, and unwrapped at a gateway that the provider runs on the edge of the IPv6 Internet.

sections.title: Private IPv4 Addresses and Number Assignment
sections.content:
Providers that give every subscriber a globally unique IPv4 address can be sure that all the IPv4-derived prefixes used with 6rd are unique. As global IPv4 addresses become scarcer, a provider may have to give customers addresses from a private IPv4 space such as 10.x.x.x, as defined in RFC 1918. Such a provider can still use 6rd. The IPv4 packets that carry IPv6 packets do not go to the address translation gateways the provider operates, because their destination is the anycast address of the 6rd relays.

In that case the 10.0.0.0/8 prefix is common to every IPv4 address in the addressing domain where 6rd is used. Knowing that, the gateways and the customer equipment could leave the constant IPv4 prefix out of the IPv6 prefixes and so reduce the IPv4 bits carried in the IPv6 prefix to 24, which did not apply to the provider described in the document. A provider large enough to serve more IPv4 endpoints than fit inside one 10.0.0.0/8 domain can also configure several such domains, each with its own 6rd relay IPv6 prefix. Each of those prefixes is the registry-allocated provider prefix followed by a domain identifier chosen by the provider.

On number assignment, the document states that providers that supply equipment to all their customers need nothing new from IANA. Being allocated an IPv6 prefix by their registry, /32 or shorter, is sufficient. If 6rd were also to be used by providers that let customers bring their own equipment, there would need to be a way to communicate the 6rd parameters to that equipment, and some number assignment would then likely be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider that cannot give every customer a public IPv4 address can still run 6rd, because the 6rd gateway address is reachable without address translation. A provider that needs several private address ranges gives each range its own 6rd prefix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for 6to4 are documented in RFC 3964. Because 6rd restricts the relays of a provider to traffic that belongs to that provider, the checks that have to be made are these.

  • For packets from customer equipment toward the Internet, the IPv6 source must be a 6rd address of the site and the IPv6 destination must not be.
  • For packets from a relay toward the Internet, the IPv6 source must be a 6rd address that matches the IPv4 source, and the IPv6 destination must not start with the provider's 6rd prefix.
  • For packets from the Internet to customer equipment, if the IPv4 source is the anycast address of the provider's own 6rd relays, the IPv6 source must not be a 6rd address of that provider. Otherwise the IPv6 source must be the 6rd address that matches the IPv4 source.
  • For packets from the Internet to a relay, the IPv6 source must not be a 6rd address of the provider, and the IPv4 destination must not be multicast, that is, must not start with 224/3. That the IPv6 destination starts with the IPv6 prefix of the provider's relays is ensured by the routing configuration, but may be double-checked.

Where IPv4 address spoofing is possible, IPv6 address spoofing is also possible, independently of these precautions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side checks that the addresses inside a packet match the rules for 6rd, so a relay only carries its own provider's traffic. Spoofing an address is still possible in the same places it is possible for IPv4.
